column4: The section links ط غ ي to water crossing its bounds; here the same verb says the water overflowed, and the people were carried in the ship, making the physical surge its clearest Quranic counterpart.
The section’s water “spurt” is named with ف ج ر; here God causes the earth to burst into springs, the waters meet, and their meeting is under a measured decree.
The section pictures punishment as the crime’s own water coming back; Noah’s people are explicitly drowned because of their sins, joining wrongdoing to the flood that overtakes them.

The section sets a burst against a protective barrier; after the flood, this ayah commands earth and sky to stop the water, which subsides and leaves the ark resting, showing a boundary re-established.

The section names water bursting as the literal branch of ف ج ر; here God makes a river flow between two gardens, a channeled, life-giving flow that clarifies the difference from floodwater overrunning its bounds.
The section’s ف ج ر begins with water bursting; here the stone yields twelve springs, and the following words assign each group its own drinking place, joining an eruption to bounded shares.
The section’s image is water escaping its bounds; here water is sent down “by measure” and lodged in the earth, a specific picture of provision contained rather than overflowing.
The section defines taqwa as a protection placed between things; this ayah says a barrier lies between the two seas and they do not transgress it, making the barrier’s holding-back function visible.

The section’s protective set holds one thing apart from another; here fresh and salt waters meet with a barrier between them, a water scene in which separation prevents one from overwhelming the other.
The section glosses taqwa as putting the self under protection from what it fears; this command explicitly tells people to guard their selves and families from the Fire.
This command to guard against the Fire gives the section’s taqwa-as-protection relation its concrete feared danger.
This ayah commands people to guard themselves from the Fire; it repeats the section’s taqwa-as-protection relation with the same concrete danger.
The section says Semūd’s taġwā is transgression and that ط غ ي can name the ruin caused by it; this ayah uses the same noun, بِالطَّاغِيَةِ, for Semūd’s destruction.
The section connects taġwā to crossing a limit and names the peoples of Ād, Semūd, and Pharaoh; this ayah says those peoples transgressed in the lands.
After the transgression named in 89:11, this ayah says they increased corruption in the lands; it makes the outward spread of the excess explicit before the punishment in 89:13.
The section’s dictionary sense says calamities can burst upon people suddenly and in quantity; this continuation of the account says the Lord poured a scourge of punishment upon the transgressors.
The section identifies فُجُور as moral bursting open into sin; here a person wants to “burst ahead” (لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ), extending that moral breach into the future.
The section names فُجُور in its moral sense; this ayah calls the sinful فُجَّار and places them in Hell, making the consequence of that moral category explicit.
The section names the moral sense of فُجُور; this ayah says the record of the فُجَّار is in Sijjīn, giving that same class a recorded consequence.
The section names ط غ ي as passing the limit in disobedience; this ayah says the human being transgresses.
The continuation specifies the trigger for the transgression in 96:6: the person sees himself as self-sufficient (اسْتَغْنَىٰ), tying overflow to imagined independence.

After the person in 96:7 sees himself as self-sufficient, this ayah says the return is to the Lord; it counters imagined independence with the accountability the section’s punishment image makes felt.
The section pairs Semūd’s transgression with Pharaoh’s and cites Moses’ mission; this command to Moses names Pharaoh as one who has طَغَىٰ.
The section sets transgression against purification; immediately after 79:17, Moses is to invite Pharaoh to تَزَكَّىٰ, giving the specific counter-direction to his excess.
Moses’ invitation in 79:18 continues with guidance to the Lord so Pharaoh may fear Him; this connects the offered purification to the section’s protection through taqwa.
The section presents taġwā as crossing the limit and sets it against restraint; this passage begins the opposite outcome with “the one who transgressed” (طَغَىٰ).
This continuation identifies the transgressor’s choice in 79:37 as preferring the nearer life; it makes the direction of the excess concrete before the consequence in 79:39.
This ayah completes the consequence of the transgression in 79:37 and the preference named in 79:38: Hell is the refuge, the return of the chosen overflow.
The section defines taqwa as a guard placed between the self and what it fears; this ayah describes the one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the soul from desire.
This ayah completes the restrained person’s outcome from 79:40 with the Garden as refuge, beside the Hell refuge of the transgressor in 79:39.
The section links Pharaoh’s ط غ ي to the moral flooding described for Semūd; here Moses and Aaron are sent to Pharaoh because he has طَغَىٰ.
Earlier in Moses’ mission, he is told to go to Pharaoh because he has طَغَىٰ; this repeats the section’s specific link between Pharaoh and transgression.
The gentle speech prescribed in 20:44 is to make Pharaoh remember or fear; it supplies the fear-facing alternative to the transgression named in 20:43.
The section says Ṣāliḥ asked Semūd to put a guard against the transgressors; this ayah gives his actual appeal, “fear God and obey me.”
This continuation says not to obey the مُسْرِفِينَ, those who exceed the measure; it is the section’s specific warning against following the people who overflow the limit.
The ayah completes Ṣāliḥ’s warning in 26:151 by saying these excess-makers spread corruption on earth and do not set things right, showing the reach of their breach.
The section names ط غ ي as exceeding a limit; here, after provision of good things, the Israelites are told not to transgress lest divine anger descend, joining a boundary to its consequence.
After the command to remain upright, this ayah says not to transgress (وَلَا تَطْغَوْا); it states the restraint that keeps the section’s moral overflow from breaking out.

The section treats ط غ ي as crossing a boundary; at the vision of the Lote Tree, the gaze “did not swerve nor transgress” (مَا زَاغَ الْبَصَرُ وَمَا طَغَىٰ), a precise contrary image of staying within bounds.
The section explains انبعاث as setting something in motion; this same noun names a departure God disliked and held back, showing that being launched into action is not itself the guarded good.

The section gives ف ج ر a physical water sense; here the rejecters demand that the Prophet cause a spring to gush from the earth, a specific request for controlled water as a sign rather than a flood.
The section’s literal water burst is echoed when springs gush from the stone; the ayah assigns each tribe its drinking place, so the source and share remain ordered.

The section evokes Noah’s overflow in 69:11; the flood account here begins with heaven’s gates opened to pouring water, supplying the sky-side of the same scene completed by the bursting earth in 54:12.
The verse stages two flowing seas meeting; 55:20 supplies the section-relevant boundary between them, so this row contributes the approaching waters that the next ayah holds apart.
In the Thamūd account, the she-camel is explicitly made a trial; this is the boundary-sign whose violation becomes the group’s transgression in the surrounding ayat.
The section’s “set” is a barrier between things; this Thamūd account assigns the camel and people their turns at the water, a concrete division they must not overrun.

The section says the worst among Thamūd bursts into action and the people follow; this account has the people call their companion, who hamstrings the camel, placing one agent’s act inside the group’s call.
After the companion’s act in 54:29, this ayah names the outcome as God’s punishment and warning, framing the transgression as a consequence rather than an isolated act.
The next ayah makes the collective end concrete: one cry leaves them like dry stalks; it completes how the single violation in 54:29 overtakes the people.

Thamūd reject the warning by asking whether they should follow “one man among us”; beside 91:12’s worst man followed by his people, this is a specific reversal between refusing a messenger and gathering around the transgressor in 54:29.
The section’s boundary image meets the Thamūd story’s water allocation: the she-camel and people each have a stated drinking turn, an ordered share that the transgressors violate.
The people hamstring the camel after the ordered drinking share in 26:155; this is the concrete breach following the section’s appeal not to follow the transgressors.
This continuation says punishment seized them; it supplies the return of the camel’s violation named in 26:157.
Ṣāliḥ sets a limit around God’s camel—leave her to graze and do not touch her with harm; the next act breaks that boundary, illustrating the protection the section associates with taqwa.
The Thamūd hamstring the camel and challenge Ṣāliḥ to bring the promised punishment; this is the decisive group act following his warning in 11:64.
After the camel is harmed, God saves Ṣāliḥ and those who believed from the disgrace of that day; this distinguishes those protected from those overtaken by the Thamūd story’s consequence.
The continuation says the wrongdoers are seized by the cry; it supplies the outward disaster following the breach in 11:65.
Ṣāliḥ identifies God’s camel as a sign and forbids harming her under threat of punishment; it is a concrete limit set before the Thamūd breach.
The Thamūd story again says they hamstrung the camel and defied their Lord’s command; it is a repeated, concrete account of the people’s transgressive choice.
The next ayah says the earthquake seized them; it completes the return from the camel’s violation in 7:77 to a collective punishment.
The account says Thamūd were shown guidance but chose blindness, then a humiliating blast seized them for what they earned; this joins refused guidance to punishment as the section does.
This continuation says God saved those who believed and were mindful of Him, making taqwa the dividing protection beside the blast in 41:17.
The Thamūd account identifies nine men who spread corruption in the land; they give a specific collective face to the “extravagant” people Ṣāliḥ warns against in 26:151.
The nine conspire to kill Ṣāliḥ and his family, turning the corruption named in 27:48 into a directed act against the messenger who warns them.
Their plot is answered by God’s counter-plan while they do not perceive it; this reverses the hidden wrongdoing of the group in 27:49.
This continuation shows the end of the nine conspirators and their people, making collective ruin follow the transgression planned in 27:49.
Among the signs of creation, this ayah names a barrier between the seas; it repeats the section’s specific image of a boundary that prevents water from simply overrunning it.
The section’s flood image is reversed by water sent down in measure to revive dead land; this is another specific Quranic picture of water held to a measure.
Pharaoh and his forces enter the sea while pursuing Israel “in rebellion and aggression”; their water-crossing carries their transgression into the setting of their drowning.
At the point of drowning, Pharaoh is told that his belief comes only now, after he disobeyed; the flood becomes the return of the excess described in the section.
The body of the drowned Pharaoh is preserved as a sign for those after him; it extends the consequence in 10:90 and 10:91 beyond the flood into a visible warning.
Pharaoh and his army act arrogantly in the land without right and assume they will not return; the section’s transgression-as-overflow is here joined to refusal of accountability.
The continuation says God seized Pharaoh and his soldiers and cast them into the sea; their landward excess returns as water carrying them away.
After the poured punishment in 89:13, this ayah says the Lord is ever watchful; it adds the accountability that makes the section’s feared boundary meaningful.

The command to guard against a trial that will not strike only its original wrongdoers gives a specific collective boundary-warning: unchecked wrongdoing can carry its effects beyond the one who began it.
The section defines taqwa as protection from what is feared; this ayah says God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day, making the protective result explicit.
The section describes taqwa as putting oneself under a shield from danger; here their Lord protects them from the punishment of Hell.
In Pharaoh’s setting, God protects the believing man from the evils of the plot against him; this gives the section’s protective sense of taqwa a concrete human danger.
This ayah says that whoever is spared the punishment of that Day has received mercy, a direct instance of the section’s protection from what is feared.

The root of taqwa also describes precaution against danger from hostile people; this ayah allows such protection as an exception to taking them as allies, making the protective boundary social and concrete.
The section sets taqwa between the self and harm; this ayah says that fearing God brings a criterion that distinguishes right from wrong, extending protection into discernment.
Pharaoh’s claim to be the highest lord is a specific expression of the transgression named for him in 79:17 and in the section’s discussion of crossing the limit.
This ayah says God seized Pharaoh as a chastening example; it supplies the consequence of the claim in 79:24 and the transgression named in 79:17.
The next ayah says Pharaoh’s fate is a lesson for the one who fears; it makes the section’s warning to restrain oneself through fear an explicit audience for this example.

Water runs through valleys in measured amounts, and a flood carries foam that disappears while what benefits people remains; this gives the section’s burst-and-barrier image a specific contrast between transient excess and lasting benefit.
In Noah’s flood, the oven’s gushing is the sign that the flood has begun; it supplies a second Quranic scene of water bursting forth before the ark carries those protected from it.
Noah’s ship runs through waves like mountains; this is a direct picture of the flood’s scale in the section’s physical-water image.

Noah’s son trusts a mountain to protect him from the water, but a wave separates and drowns him; his failed refuge contrasts with the ark’s protection in 11:42 and the section’s shield against danger.
This retelling pairs the oven’s gushing with the command to load the ark; it is another specific account of bursting floodwater and the refuge prepared against it.

People describe Gog and Magog as corruptors on earth and ask Dhul-Qarnayn to build a barrier between them and the people; this directly stages protection placed between a feared force and those it threatens.
Dhul-Qarnayn accepts the task of making a barrier; this supplies his answer to the request in 18:94 and turns the section’s protective boundary into a built one.
This ayah describes the iron and molten-copper construction of the barrier requested in 18:94, making the act of setting a firm boundary concrete.
Gog and Magog cannot climb over or pierce the completed barrier; its own contribution is the protection that keeps the corrupters from crossing into the people’s space.
Dhul-Qarnayn says the barrier is a mercy but will be leveled when God’s promise comes; this marks the protection as a boundary that will eventually be removed.
Once that barrier is removed, people surge against one another; this is the section’s image of an unchecked flow made social and visible.
The release of Gog and Magog sends them rushing down from every height; it repeats the section’s image of transgression breaking outward once restraint is gone.

This continuation explains the harmful movement withheld in 9:46: if those people had set out, they would have rushed among the community spreading confusion and sedition, a specific case of bad movement spreading to others.

The section warns against following the musrifin, those who exceed limits; this ayah describes God’s servants as neither extravagant nor miserly in spending, giving a concrete picture of the restraint between excess and deficiency.
This ayah commands people to eat and drink without excess; it repeats the section’s warning against the musrifin as a limit on consumption.
The command not to obey a person who follows desire and exceeds bounds parallels Salih’s warning not to follow the musrifin, making the danger of following an unrestrained leader specific.

The section presents fujur as releasing the self into disobedience; this ayah says that if truth followed people’s desires, the heavens and earth would be corrupted, showing the scale of disorder that unchecked desire would produce.
Qarun is told not to seek corruption in the land; this echoes Salih’s specific command not to follow those who spread corruption and makes restraint an answer to transgression.
Qarun claims his wealth came from his own knowledge, a concrete form of the self-sufficiency that the section links to human transgression and that 96:7 names as its trigger.
The earth swallows Qarun and his dwelling after his boast; the land itself takes the overreaching person down, a specific reversal of the section’s image of overflow returning upon its source.
On the Day of Judgment a wall separates the believers from the hypocrites, with mercy on one side and punishment on the other; it gives the section’s protective boundary a specific moral division.
